Hawaii’s food system is currently in a difficult position. The reason behind this is that we live on an island, we rely on ships and planes for almost everything we eat. According to the Department of Agriculture and Biosecurity (2026), Hawaii imported about 233.8 million dollars' worth of food in 2024. This dependency is a major risk because if shipping is ever delayed by a storm or by a global crisis, our food supply could easily run out in just a few days. Which makes living here really expensive. In 2026, Honolulu was ranked as the most expensive city in the U.S. for groceries with residents paying 31% more than the national average (Cheapism, 2026). By growing organic food locally, we can lower these costs and make sure our community always has access to fresh produce.

Boosting local farming is also the best way to help Hawaii’s economy. Right now, the state relies heavily on tourism, which makes up about 21% of our economy (Department of Agriculture and Biosecurity, 2026). If fewer people visit Hawaii, the whole state suffers. By using technology to grow and export high-value local plants, we can create a more stable economy with good-paying jobs that don’t depend on tourists.

One of the biggest problems we face is that our farmers are getting older. Recent data shows that there are over 5,600 farmers in Hawaii aged 65 or older, but only 765 farmers under the age of 35 (Department of Agriculture and Biosecurity,2025). As these older farmers retire, we are losing the people we need to grow our food. Our project uses robotics and AI to help solve this “labor gap” . We aren't trying to replace workers; we are building tools that allow fewer people to do more work, helping the next generation of farmers keep up with demand.
The main issue we are focusing on is making “Controlled-Environment Agriculture” (like high-tech greenhouses) work for Hawaii. Research shows that using these systems can

increase crop yields by five times while tutting the use of pesticides by 50% (University of Hawaii CTAHR, 2026). However, these systems are hard to manage and need constant attention to prevent problems like “tip burn” in lettuce or water chemistry changes. Our project which combines robotic arms, smart cameras, and sensors creates an automated “safety net” for farmers. This technology makes local organic farming easier, more productive and more profitable for the people of Hawaii.

Rather than servos, this assembly uses a single stepper motor that drives a linear motion screw, allowing the carriage to move up and down, which retracts/extends the fingers depending on the direction of motion of the carriage.

The first task was to design the assembly itself, which was created on Onshape and 3D printed. The design is highly reminiscent of an arcade claw machine, using a similar cantilever mechanism to prevent the central carriage from spinning whilst the stepper motor is being driven.
The printed assembly was of standard PLA plastic, and the fingers were printed using TPU for flexibility while maintaining rigidity.

Some hardware was required. Several M2 threaded shoulder bolts were used to attach the beams and fingers to the “core” and central carriage, with nyLock bolts and nylon washers to prevent slipping while in motion.
Figure: (1) Render of assembly, (2) Physical assembly attached to the table
Next, we must consider the electronics. The most important aspect is the motor and its controls.

The motor selected was the stepper motor with model number 17HE15-1504S. This is a bipolar two-phase stepper motor, which is designed for high torque and operational efficiency. It is composed of two individual coils that drive the motor assembly.
The motor runs at 1.5 amps of input current at a potential of 12 volts, as specified in the motor driver specification sheet and the stepper motor data sheet.
Figure: (1) Physical dimensions with pinouts, (2) Schematic symbol of this particular motor.

To interface between a computer system and the motor itself, an interlink is required. This is fulfilled by the use of a motor driver. For this design, we utilized the Big Easy Driver (ver 1.2), which was designed by Brian Schmalz, and the PCB was manufactured by Sparkfun Electronics.
Figure: Big Easy Stepper Driver PCB

This PCB supplies more than enough current, capable of handling up to 2A of current per phase, and the actual current can be controlled by a screw-operated potentiometer built into the PCB, allowing current to range from 0 amps per phase up to 2 amps per phase. It can handle up to 35 V for the motor drive voltage, but 12V DC is sufficient for this motor.
The actual operating principle of this board is described as follows:

This board is supplied by 12 volts DC through the M+ and GND pins. Then, the DIR pin is either pulled to high or low (alternates between 0V and 5V square-waveform). Depending on whether a high or low voltage signal is applied to this pin will change the direction of the stepper motor. The signal for DIR is sampled upon the rising edge of the STP pin.

The STP pin is the most important here. The STP pin takes between 0V and 5V (Peak), where alternating between 0 and 5V causes one step to be taken (also called a rising edge). This pin can be continuously driven at high frequencies (or very small delays by the relationship f = 1/T) for seamless motor control.

For this gripper, we do not utilize the microstep function of this board for simplicity’s sake, though it is wired between the Arduino and the controller if it is indeed needed for the future; we have found that using the STP pin alone is sufficient for smooth movement.

Finally, there are also several other mandatory pins, which include the EN (enable pin), pulling this pin low allows for control, while if pulled high disables all other outputs. VCC and GND are unnecessary, as this is basically just 5V from the PCB that can be used to power other components (at small currents)

The Arduino allows a computer to interface with the motor driver and sends a digital signal to the controller, allowing the motor to operate depending on the frequency of the pulses and whether the signal is high or low.

The Arduino board that was selected is a third-party board, called the Red Board, manufactured by Sparkfun Electronics. It uses the same chip as the Arduino Uno, but with some improvements, such as a lack of exposed solder joints due to the entire PCB having surface-mounted components.
Because the Big Easy Driver board’s logic is controlled by a digital signal, the STP, EN, DIR, and MS1-3 terminals are connected to the digital pins of the Arduino (namely digital pins 3-8).

This allows us to give a constant value to a variable before compilation and is very memory efficient.

Sometimes it is cumbersome to control the motor through the serial monitor on the Arduino IDE. To resolve this problem, a simple GUI wrapper was developed to help reduce the frustration often seen when dealing with terminal-based scripts.
The two main Python packages utilized were customtkinter (GUI) and pySerial (establishes a serial connection over USB).
It is unnecessary to completely describe the code itself, as the Python project itself is completely optional and is not required to operate the gripper.
The program itself has some safety features, such as preventing the user from sending signals to the Arduino while the motor is in operation, amongst others.

Due to time constraints, the gripper and code were developed over three weeks (started mid-April and completed on May 6th). So there were not many opportunities to test the gripper. However, we were able to quickly test if the gripper properly functioned by having it grasp a lettuce.

From testing the gripper, we noticed that the gripper was able to grasp itself, although the motor stalled quickly when slight pressure was applied to the lettuce. This is strange, as the motor itself is not underperformant and is capable of exerting fairly high torques. This could be attributed to the limited current, as using a DMM (digital multimeter), we observed that the maximum current through the entire circuit (from hot to ground) was only 600 mA, which was well below the rated spec of the stepper motor. Upon further analysis, we discovered the motor controller board had a faulty potentiometer. Even when turning the potentiometer both fully clockwise and counterclockwise, the current supplied will not budge past 600 mA.

The motor was also loud, and there was a significant grinding noise heard as the carriage moved up and down the screw. However, linear motion is still smooth, and this noise can be reduced by applying a lubricant, but still worthy to mention as having a noisy gripper is suboptimal.

The motor control board also ran hot, with it being nearly impossible to handle with bare hands. In the future, this issue can be mitigated by cooling the central IC with a thermal pad and/or heatsink. This heat, however, does not affect the performance, and the board can comfortably handle up to 2.2A without requiring external cooling.

The Arduino code and Python code worked well together, and there were no real issues or latency. Of course, with the development of any software product, bugs are absolutely expected, and this project is no exception. Over the course of development, many bugs were encountered, such as large delays when driving the STP pin, which was due to many cycles being sucked up by an errant serial print function being mistakenly appended into a for loop.

Overall, this design served as the successor to R1A, and even in the midst of time constraints, we were able to come up with a working model and some code to follow along. It was able to grasp a head of lettuce, albeit very poorly, which can be attributed to current-limiting by the motor controller board because of a faulty potentiometer. We were successful in reducing the motor count from three to one, and we plan to use the code developed for this gripper as a base for our next iteration of this project, namely, avoiding the use of fingers entirely.

What to Look for in Choosing a Camera

The purpose of calculating megapixels and field of view (FOV) for each camera setup is to determine how much of the scene the camera can capture and how detailed the image will be. In this analysis, the main focus is on FOV, since it shows the physical area visible to the camera. A larger FOV allows more of the environment to be seen, while a smaller FOV provides a more zoomed-in and detailed view of a smaller area. By comparing different setups, the goal is to find a balance between capturing enough of the scene and maintaining sufficient image clarity. Based on the results, the selected camera setup is the one that provides a reasonable FOV without excessive distortion, while still maintaining adequate resolution for clear observation.

To determine the appropriate cameras, the workspace (left section) was first measured to be approximately 1.022 m × 1.212 m × 1.257 m, with a corner-to-corner distance of 1.702 m. These values were used as the target field of view (FOV) needed for each camera setup.

FOV data was collected using an Innomaker 1080P and Innomaker 720P USB camera with different lenses (standard, 2.8 mm, and 180° fisheye). A beam level was placed in the camera view, and a scale factor was calculated using: real length ÷ pixel length. This scale was then used to convert image pixel dimensions into real-world FOV width and height.

The main factor used to determine camera selection was whether the FOV width and height matched or slightly exceeded the workspace dimensions (~1.02 m × 1.21 m). Setups with smaller FOV could not capture the full area, while fisheye lenses provided more coverage with some distortion.
The middle of the setup uses an Innomaker 1080P with a 2.8 mm lens for full workspace coverage with clear detail.
The training arm uses an Innomaker 1080P with a fisheye lens to capture a wide view of the gripper and lettuce.
The corner of the setup uses an Innomaker 720P with a 2.8 mm lens to provide additional coverage and reduce blind spots.

This section focused on designing a multi-camera system for the robotic arm and workspace. The workspace was measured first, and field of view (FOV) data was collected using Innomaker 1080P and 720P cameras with different lenses and distances. A ruler-based method was used to convert pixel measurements into real-world FOV values to compare each setup with the workspace size. Camera choices were made based on which setups best matched the workspace dimensions while maintaining clear image quality. The 1080P camera with a 2.8 mm lens was used for the main view, the fisheye lens for the training arm to capture wide motion, and the 720P camera for corner coverage to reduce blind spots. Overall, the system provides full coverage, stable mounting, and clear views for tracking robot movement.

During the calibration process, the range of motion of each motor, under a 12-bit resolution, in both leader and follower arms are recorded and converted into a range from -100 to 100. Connected in a daisy chain, the ST3215 motors each have a unique motor ID and only receives signals from its counterpart in the other arm during teleoperation. Maintaining the single motor controller and three-pronged follower gripper design, the software must be capable of sending the positional information of one motor to three motors rather than the original one to one. This can be accomplished by directly updating the motor positions to that of the controller, without relying on the one to one set up before.

While the follower arm may have joints that contain multiple motors in order to increase its carrying capacity, the leader arm remains the same in all cases. A multi-motor joint requires the two motors to face in opposite directions, while also receiving the same command from a single motor in the follower arm, meaning that the command must be updated within the script before it is sent to the follower. If calibrated properly, this can theoretically be accomplished by reversing the signum of its positional command.
